title: Index signatures and Record<K, V>
hook: An index signature types dynamic string keys on an object — like a dictionary of HTTP headers or translation strings. Record<K, V> is the built-in shorthand, but noUncheckedIndexedAccess changes whether lookups are T or T | undefined.

blocks.text: An **index signature** declares that an object accepts arbitrary keys of a given type mapping to a value type: `{ [key: string]: number }`. **`Record<K, V>`** is sugar for `{ [P in K]: V }` — a mapped type over keys. At **run time** JavaScript objects are still plain hashes — no key validation. **`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`** makes `obj[key]` return `V | undefined` because the key might not exist. Contrast C# `Dictionary<string, T>` which throws on missing keys unless you use `TryGetValue`.

entries.plainDefinition: Types all string (or number/symbol) keys on an object to the same value type.
Built-in mapped type for key-value dictionaries with known key union.
Compiler flag: indexed access adds undefined to the result type.

blocks.text: API configs, i18n maps, and Redux-style action lookup tables all use dynamic keys. Using `any` or untyped objects loses safety — index signatures document the contract. Senior interviews ask when to prefer **discriminated unions** over stringly-typed Records. C# developers reach for Dictionary — TypeScript Records are compile-time only.

blocks.title: Prefer known keys when possible
blocks.body: Record<"pending" | "done", Handler> is safer than Record<string, Handler> — exhaustiveness checking applies.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Fixed key set
items.body: Use Record<UnionOfKeys, V> or mapped type — compiler enforces all keys.

items.title: Open-ended keys
items.body: Use index signature [key: string]: V — any string key allowed.

items.title: Mixed fixed + dynamic
items.body: Known props + index signature — excess property rules apply to literals.

items.title: Safe lookup
items.body: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess, guard: if (key in obj) { ... }

diagram.title: Index signature vs Record
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  NEED[Need dictionary type] --> FIXED{Known key union?}
  FIXED -->|yes| REC[Record K V]
  FIXED -->|no| IDX["[key: string]: V"]
  REC --> EXH[Exhaustiveness on K]
  IDX --> OPEN[Any string key]

blocks.title: Record<string, T> everywhere
blocks.body: Loses exhaustiveness — prefer union keys or branded keys for domain IDs.

blocks.text: Index signatures interact with excess property checking: literals cannot have unknown keys unless an index signature is present. `as const` objects can be indexed with keyof typeof for safer lookups. For API query params, validate keys at runtime — Record types do not enforce keys exist. Branded string types (UserId) prevent accidental cross-wiring of Record keys.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs
rows: Key union must stay in sync

blocks.title: What gets you rejected
blocks.body: Saying Record enforces keys at runtime. Not knowing noUncheckedIndexedAccess. Using any for dynamic objects instead of index signatures.

interviewTakeaways: Index signatures type open-ended object keys; Record<K,V> types known key unions.
Runtime: still plain objects — undefined for missing keys.
noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds undefined to indexed lookups.
60s: Use Record<Union,V> for finite keys with exhaustiveness. Index signature for open maps. Guard lookups. C# Dictionary throws; JS/TS return undefined.
commonPitfalls: Weak: Record<string, T> for everything — loses key safety.
Weak: assuming indexed access always returns T — missing keys are undefined.
Strong: Union-key Record for enums/status. Index signature for open maps. in-check or ?? for safe access.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS objects accept any string key at runtime — TypeScript index signatures document that pattern at compile time.
Record<K,V> is built on mapped types — same machinery as Partial and Pick.
